question: Can long-lived acquisition recover with one scalar per graph, one incoming-weight radius per neuron, or a compact unsigned-magnitude and signed-direction birth scaffold?
choice: Make the candidate choice on original six births and fixed calibration worlds before inspecting independent results. Primary score is all of A, B and novel X after four A/B studies and 16, 64, 128 later contacts in which A is absent. Also measure each individual answer and the recurring environment.
arms: native: every weight, bias, growth and retirement is open and applied as usual.
global_radius: after the native edit, softly restore only the joint Euclidean norm of all expressed weights and biases to its birth value.
row_radius: do this independently for each receiving neuron, treating bias as an additional incoming coordinate. It uses 20 reference values and no ancestral mask.

signed_rows: restore each still-present birth address towards sign(birth) times that row's birth RMS of nonzero entries including bias. Store 420 ternary signs in 105 packed bytes plus 20 fp32 row amplitudes. A re-grown original address is eligible again. No mutable ancestry mask.
indexed_exact: same address rule as signed_rows with full birth magnitudes. This isolates loss of directional magnitude information from the address eligibility change.
control: Compare native actions reconstructed on the same cue, law, motor and edit tape with the archived native slow-reference study. Measure the difference between a compact reference and the full static lifelong reference on the same physical histories. All interventions retain native support changes and incoming numeric updates at every contact.
limitations: Compressed byte counts refer to inherited reference content. Temporary reconstruction tensors for batched CPU evaluation, and the ordinary live graph, are additional. These are external physical update interventions. A successful fixed radius would not establish that the graph spontaneously discovered one.
